Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a comparison of two approaches to background jobs: a queue with workers, and scheduled batch runs. Around 200 words.

A queue with workers takes a job the moment a worker is free. Submit a task and a worker picks it up in seconds, processes it, and moves to the next one. This suits work that arrives unpredictably: image resizing after an upload, sending a welcome email after signup, charging a card after checkout. The tradeoff is operational: you run a persistent worker pool, size it against queue depth, and handle retries and dead-letter queues when a job fails partway through.

Scheduled batch runs wait for a fixed time and then process everything that accumulated: a nightly report, a weekly billing reconciliation, a daily data sync. There's no standing worker fleet — a cron trigger starts a process, it runs to completion, and it exits. This costs less when work doesn't need to happen right away, and it makes debugging simpler because each run has a clear start and end with one log to check.

The choice comes down to latency and volume. If users wait on the result, use a queue. If the data only needs to be current as of tomorrow morning, a scheduled run does the same work for less infrastructure. Some systems use both: a queue for real-time actions like order confirmation, and a nightly batch job for aggregation that doesn't need to be live.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a paragraph on what happens when a job fails in each.

A queue with workers takes a job the moment a worker is free. Submit a task and a worker picks it up in seconds, processes it, and moves to the next one. This suits work that arrives unpredictably: image resizing after an upload, sending a welcome email after signup, charging a card after checkout. The tradeoff is operational: you run a persistent worker pool, size it against queue depth, and handle retries and dead-letter queues when a job fails partway through.

When a job fails in a queue system, the message stays in the queue and a worker retries it, usually with backoff, until it either succeeds or hits a retry limit. Past that limit it moves to a dead-letter queue for inspection, while the rest of the queue keeps flowing around it. A single bad job can be isolated without stopping other work.

Scheduled batch runs wait for a fixed time and then process everything that accumulated: a nightly report, a weekly billing reconciliation, a daily data sync. There's no standing worker fleet: a cron trigger starts a process, it runs to completion, and it exits. This costs less when work doesn't need to happen right away, and it makes debugging simpler because each run has a clear start and end with one log to check.

A batch failure is coarser. If the process crashes partway through, the whole run is often incomplete or partially applied, and the fix is usually to make the job idempotent so rerunning it from scratch is safe. Some batch systems checkpoint progress so a retry resumes where it left off, but that has to be built in; it doesn't come free the way per-message retry does in a queue.

The choice comes down to latency and volume. If users wait on the result, use a queue. If the data only needs to be current as of tomorrow morning, a scheduled run does the same work for less infrastructure. Some systems use both: a queue for real-time actions like order confirmation, and a nightly batch job for aggregation that doesn't need to be live.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a recommendation for a small team.

A queue works well for a small team when someone needs to see the result quickly and the team doesn't want to run a nightly script by hand. A managed queue like SQS, Cloud Tasks, or Sidekiq backed by Redis keeps the operational load low: one or two worker processes, autoscaled or not, cover most workloads. Reserve the batch approach for the handful of jobs that are naturally daily or weekly, like a report or reconciliation, and run those on the same infrastructure with a simple cron trigger rather than standing up a separate scheduling system. A team with a few hundred background jobs a day rarely needs both a queue and a batch framework from day one; start with a queue for anything user-facing, add scheduled runs only when a specific job is clearly periodic, and avoid building retry or checkpoint logic until a job has actually failed in a way that matters.
